turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. I've brought Mr Hale through. I've done the lying and standing pressures, and I'll read them whenever you're ready.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, just hold them a moment. Come in, Mr Hale, take a seat. Your daughter rang the rooms yesterday, quite concerned.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Good morning, Doctor. Elaine does worry more than is necessary. I assured her I was perfectly well, but she would not be dissuaded.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): She said you'd fallen twice, and that you go dizzy whenever you stand.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I did not fall, Doctor. I slid, if a word is required. And I am not dizzy. I shouldn't like you to think I am unsteady on my feet.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. Tell me what happened the first time, as you remember it.
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): I was in the kitchen, reaching for a cup, and my legs simply... they went from under me, and I slid down the cupboard. I was not thrown. I...
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Were you hurt?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): No, not at all. I got myself up, a little embarrassed, and that was the end of it.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the second time?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Rising from the toilet. I slid onto the bath mat. No harm done. I live on my own in the unit, so when Elaine found me there she made rather a scene.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can you put a date on either one?
[SEG0013] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry to butt in. If I don't give you these figures now I'll lose the bit of paper.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Of course, go on.

[SEG0015] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Lying blood pressure one hundred and forty-eight over eighty-two, pulse seventy-two. Standing, after about a minute, one hundred and sixteen over seventy, pulse ninety-four. Saturation ninety-seven percent on room air.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. That's a sizeable drop. I'm already wondering whether the tablets are behind it, but I want the rest of the story. Mr Hale, any dates?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): I couldn't tell you the day, I'm afraid. Sometime after the long weekend, I believe, though I would not swear to it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And between those episodes, any light-headed spells through the day?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I really don't believe so.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. You seemed about to say something else about that weekend.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): My grandson had me in front of the cricket the whole Sunday. He is quite mad about it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Who were we playing?
[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): India, the day match. He explained every field placement at considerable length, and I nodded as though I understood.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Did we win? I've been stuck on call, I haven't seen a ball bowled.
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): We did, off the last over, which he found extremely satisfactory. He then insisted on ice cream, and there was none in the freezer.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): The weather has been kind for sitting about, at least.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): It has. Warm, without that dreadful heat we had in January. Elaine arrived with scones. Far too many scones.
[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha. Let me bring you back, though. Getting out of the chair, or up off the toilet, what did you actually feel?
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): Well. If I am to be honest, Doctor, there is a moment. The room does not spin, exactly. It goes dim, and I must hold the bench until it passes.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0031] person_3 (PATIENT): A few weeks, I should say. Mostly when I get up too quickly. If I sit still, it settles in a moment.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it, tightness, or pain in the arm?
[SEG0033] person_3 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Do you black out, or lose consciousness at all?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): No. I have always known where I am.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Palpitations? The heart racing or thumping?
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): No, I have not noticed that.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any headaches, or trouble with the waterworks or the bowels?
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): No headaches. Waterworks and bowels are quite regular, thank you.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have you ever had an operation?
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): None. I have been fortunate in that respect.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Allergies to any medicines?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): No, none that I am aware of.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me the tablets you take. The blood pressure ones, and the one for sleep.
[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Perindopril in the morning, five milligrams, I believe. Amlodipine ten milligrams, also each morning. Both for the blood pressure.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): And there was a beta blocker once, wasn't there?
[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): Atenolol, fifty milligrams. I stopped it in March. It made me feel rather slowed, and you were happy for me to leave it off.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the sleeping tablet?
[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): Temazepam, ten milligrams, meant to be every night. I skip it if I have already nodded off in the chair. I could not say how often I miss it.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): There was also a script for rosuvastatin, after the cholesterol result. Did you ever start that?
[SEG0051] person_3 (PATIENT): I never took it. I never even collected it from the chemist. I hope that is not a problem.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not a problem. We'll park the cholesterol. No bruises on the arms or the hips that I can see. Pulse is regular while you're sitting. Chest is clear.
[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): I have had the high blood pressure for years, as you know.

[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, that is ongoing. I think this is a postural drop from the tablets, and the amlodipine is the one I would ease first. I can't completely rule out an inner-ear problem, but the readings fit the blood pressure much better.
[SEG0055] person_3 (PATIENT): I see. I should still like the pressure treated, if that remains wise.

[SEG0056] person_2 (DOCTOR): We keep treating it, only more gently. We'll bring the amlodipine down from ten milligrams to five milligrams each morning. Carry on with the perindopril. Stay with the temazepam as you have been, and don't add any other sleeping tablet.
[SEG0057] person_3 (PATIENT): Five milligrams. Shall I begin this evening, or wait for the morning?

[SEG0058] person_2 (DOCTOR): From tomorrow morning. I'll write the new script. When you get up, sit on the edge of the bed and count to twenty before you stand, and if it dims, hold the bench and sit again. Keep your fluids up in this weather, and please tell Elaine about the change.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): I shall do all of that. She will be glad it has been attended to.
[SEG0060] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange a blood test for your kidney function and electrolytes, and an ECG today if you can fit him in before he leaves.
[SEG0061] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): We can do the ECG at the desk on the way out. Easy done.
[SEG0062] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in a fortnight, and we'll check the standing pressure again.
[SEG0063] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, Doctor. Elaine can bring me.
[SEG0064] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you black out or have another slide before then, don't wait for the fortnight, come straight back.
[SEG0065] person_3 (PATIENT): I understand. Thank you for explaining it so carefully, and for your time.
[SEG0066] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome, Mr Hale. Go carefully on the way out.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.reason: Twice supported, but certainty is wrong; patient states slides clearly, not uncertainly.
bad.text: sliding to the floor (category=other, status=present, frequency=twice, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)
